title: How to Care for Creation as a Christian
excerpt: The first job God gave a human being was to tend a garden. Caring for creation is not a borrowed cause from the culture. It is the oldest assignment in the Bible.
body:
Before there was a temple, a law, or a single commandment about worship, there was a garden and a gardener. God put the man in Eden to work it and keep it, and the word translated keep is the same word used for guarding and protecting. The first vocation given to a human being was the care of a place. This is not a modern cause grafted onto the faith. It is in the opening pages, written into what a human being is for.

We have largely lost this, and we lost it for a reason worth naming. The moment creation care comes up, an alarm sounds, because the subject has been captured by the American argument, sorted into a partisan column, and most believers have decided it must therefore belong to the other side. We let a political fight tell us which parts of Genesis to ignore.

## The earth is the Lord's, not ours

The Psalmist says the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. This single line dismantles two errors at once. Against the one who thinks the world is ours to use up however we please, it says the world belongs to God, not to us, and we are stewards who will give an account. Against the one who wants to worship the creation itself, it says the earth is the Lord's, his handiwork, to be honored as a gift and not adored as a god. The Christian neither plunders the world nor deifies it. He keeps it, as a trust from its Maker.

Dominion, the word God gave the man, has been badly abused to mean domination. But the dominion of God's image-bearer is meant to mirror God's own rule, which feeds the ravens, clothes the lilies, and notices the sparrow that falls. To have dominion the way God does is to care, to cultivate, to make a place flourish, not to strip it bare and walk away.

## Creation is not yours to exhaust

The law built rhythms of rest into the land itself. Every seventh year the fields were to lie fallow, the soil allowed to recover. This was not sentimentality. It was a structural refusal to treat the creation as an endless resource to be squeezed until it failed. The God of the law would not let his people exhaust the ground any more than he would let them exhaust the poor. Both bore his concern. Both had limits he commanded his people to honor.

This cuts against a way of living that treats consumption as limitless and consequence as someone else's problem. The Christian who believes the earth is the Lord's cannot be casual about wasting it, fouling it, or handing his children a depleted version of the gift he was given. Stewardship has a time horizon longer than my own convenience.

## Creation groans, and waits

Paul says the whole creation groans, subjected to futility, waiting for its redemption alongside the children of God. The Christian hope is not that the world will be discarded while souls float off to heaven. It is that creation itself will be renewed, that there will be a new heavens and a new earth. This matters enormously for how we treat the world now. If the material creation is destined for the trash, you can use it up. If it is destined for redemption, it is to be honored now as a thing God has not given up on.

That is why creation care is not a distraction from the gospel. It is a sign of it, a small foretaste of the day when all things are made new, lived out in advance by people who refuse to treat God's good world as disposable.

## Refuse the partisan frame

Here the partisan capture has to be named and refused directly. One tribe has made creation care a flag, and another has made denial of it a loyalty test, and the believer is told he must pick a team. The ancient Christian ethic predates both teams by millennia. It does not arrive at creation care through a party platform. It arrives through Genesis, the Psalms, the law, and Paul. Tend the garden because God told the first human to, not because a party told you to, and not refusing to tend it because a different party told you not to.

## This week

Pick one concrete, unglamorous act of keeping the garden, and do it as worship rather than politics. Waste less of something. Tend a piece of ground, a tree, a patch of land near you. Repair instead of replace. Refuse one habit of careless consumption you have justified because everyone does it. Do it quietly, as the oldest assignment in the Bible, given to a gardener in a garden long before there was a party to argue about it.
